children: The Bank of Israel cut short-term interest rates for the third straight time on Tuesday — and to the lowest level in nearly four years — as price pressures remained contained, helped by a strong shekel

In contrast to tighter monetary policy globally, Israel's central bank reduced its benchmark rate (ILINR=ECI) to 3.25%, its lowest level since late 2022, from 3.50%. It had cut rates in November and January, then paused due to the conflict with Iran and fears of a spike in supply-driven inflation, and then resumed cuts in May and July.
Tuesday's move was not the majority view in a Reuters poll: Eight of 14 economists had expected no change in rates, while the other six backed a 25 basis-point cut.
The annual inflation rate stood at 1.5% in July, well within the bank's 1% to 3% target range.
"Inflation has moderated in recent months, and its rate ... was lower than the midpoint of the target range," the Bank of Israel said in a statement.

It noted that while Israel's economy had bounced back in the second quarter, growing an annualised 15.4%, "net of production abroad by Israeli companies, GDP in the second quarter was (just) 3.8 percent higher than in the fourth quarter of 2025 in annual terms."

"The Monetary Committee’s policy is focusing on price stability, support for economic activity, and stability of the markets," it said. "The interest rate path will be determined in accordance with the development of inflation, economic activity, geopolitical uncertainty, and fiscal developments."
The central bank previously has forecast a rates floor of about 3% by mid-2027.
